chief_complaint: arm/elbow clenched tightly, spastic catch on passive stretch
hpi_details: A 41-year-old male with residual right-sided weakness after a prior stroke presents with gradually worsening elbow-flexor tightness and a velocity-dependent catch on passive stretch. The stiffness interferes with hand hygiene and dressing; he denies sudden new weakness, facial droop, or speech difficulty.
ideas: He thinks the muscles and tendons in his elbow are shrinking and knotting up because he hasn't been stretching them enough since his stroke.
concerns: He is worried that his clenched fingers will dig into his palm and cause a skin infection, or that he will lose the ability to dress himself.
expectations: He hopes to get muscle-relaxing injections or medication and targeted stretching exercises so he can open his hand to wash it.
pmh: Prior stroke with residual right-sided weakness

clinical_knowledge.topic: Post-Stroke Spastic Hemiplegia evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Post-Stroke Spastic Hemiplegia is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Management begins with identifying reversible triggers, setting functional goals, and using positioning, splinting, and therapist-guided range-of-motion. Consider focal botulinum toxin injection for function-limiting focal spasticity after specialist assessment.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: arm/elbow clenched tightly, spastic catch on passive stretch

Key HPI features: A 41-year-old male presents to the clinic with arm/elbow clenched tightly, spastic catch on passive stretch. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Post-Stroke Spasticity.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Post-Stroke Spastic Hemiplegia.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Parkinsonian rigidity without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Severe flexor contractures.
management_principles: Assess for pain, infection, skin breakdown, constipation, or bladder problems that may worsen spasticity, and use therapist-guided positioning, splinting, and range-of-motion.
Refer to rehabilitation medicine or neurology for function-limiting spasticity, contracture, or consideration of focal botulinum toxin; urgent evaluation is required for sudden new focal deficits.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: Upper motor neuron lesion following stroke causing velocity-dependent hypertonia and muscle spasms.
red_flags: Sudden new weakness, facial droop, speech difficulty, or severe new headache

must_ask.say: Does your arm or leg feel tight and snap back when you try to straighten it quickly?

must_ask.objective: Functional impact on hygiene and dressing
must_ask.say: Does the stiffness interfere with washing your palm or putting on clothes?
Do you experience sudden, painful muscle spasms in your leg at night?
Are you taking medications like baclofen or have you received Botox injections?
When did your stroke occur and how has the stiffness progressed since then?

history.answer: Ever since my stroke, my right arm has had some weakness, but recently my elbow and hand have been curling up tight and stiffening up.
The stiffness started creeping in about two months ago and has been gradually getting tighter and tighter over the past few weeks.
It is located in my right arm, primarily keeping my right elbow bent and my wrist and fingers curled toward my chest.
It feels like a continuous, tight muscle knot or clamp that strongly resists whenever I try to straighten the arm.
If I or someone else tries to pull the arm straight quickly, it suddenly catches and locks up, but it gives way if stretched very slowly.
I get sudden, painful muscle cramps or spasms about three or four times a day, particularly when I yawn or get startled.
The muscles feel constantly fatigued and achy from clenching, but there is no deep bone or joint ache.
Cold temperatures, stress, and moving suddenly make it tighter, whereas a warm bath and slow, gentle stretching loosen it slightly.
I have been experiencing generalized fatigue because doing everyday tasks takes so much extra effort, but my left side feels completely normal.
No, I have not experienced any sudden new weakness, facial droop, numbness, speech difficulties, or sudden severe headaches.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, or night sweats.
No, the skin in my palm and elbow crease has not cracked or developed sores, though it gets sweaty and hard to clean.
I had an ischemic stroke eight months ago that caused weakness on my right side, and I spent two months doing inpatient rehabilitation.
I am not currently taking any muscle relaxants or prescription medications for this muscle tightness.
I tried doing the home stretching exercises my therapist taught me, but the arm has become too tight for me to open it on my own.
It has become very difficult to wash my right armpit and palm, and putting on a shirt or buttoning clothes is a huge struggle.
I am currently on medical leave from my office desk job, and the muscle tightness occasionally wakes me up if I roll onto my right side.
My rehabilitation therapist mentioned that muscle tightness called spasticity can happen after a stroke, so I think that might be what this is.
I'm scared that my fingers will dig so hard into my palm that the skin breaks and gets infected, or that I won't be able to dress myself anymore.
I was hoping there is a muscle-relaxing injection or pill you can give me so I can open my hand enough to clean it.
Aside from the stroke eight months ago and the weakness it left on my right side, I have no other chronic medical conditions.
I was hospitalized for two weeks when the stroke occurred followed by rehab, but I have never had any surgeries.
I am not taking any prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or dietary supplements at this time.
No, I have no known allergies to any medications, foods, or latex.
No, I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products.
I drink one or two beers on social occasions once or twice a month, but nothing heavy.
I work as an office accountant and live in an apartment with my wife, who helps assist me with meals and hygiene.
My father had high blood pressure and passed away from a stroke in his late seventies, while my mother is alive and healthy.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, heart rate 72 bpm, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, temperature 36.6 C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert, comfortable at rest, sitting with the right upper extremity held in adduction, elbow flexion, and wrist pronation.
Pupils equal and reactive, extraocular movements intact, mild residual right lower facial flattening from prior stroke, speech clear, and tongue midline.
Increased muscle tone with clasp-knife spasticity in right elbow flexors and finger flexors; strength is 4/5 throughout the right side and 5/5 on the left.
Velocity-dependent catch upon rapid passive extension of the right elbow, but full passive range of motion is achieved with slow stretch without fixed contractures.
Hyperactive deep tendon reflexes at right biceps and patella (3+) with an extensor plantar response on the right; normal 2+ reflexes on the left.
Skin in the right palmar creases, antecubital fossa, and axilla is clean and intact without maceration, erythema, or breakdown.
Mild right hemiparetic circumducting gait with reduced right arm swing; no ataxia noted on the left side.
No resting tremor, cogwheel rigidity, fasciculations, or involuntary movements noted.
